title: What Greek temple columns were really holding up
description: The rows of columns on a Greek temple look like decoration, but they are the building's skeleton: a stone post-and-lintel system carrying a heavy roof, one upright at a time.

body.heading: Posts, beams and a stone roof
paragraphs: A Greek temple is built like a giant stone table. The columns are the legs, standing in rows around a central room; across their tops runs a horizontal beam called the architrave, and above that sat the roof structure and the triangular pediment at each end.

Stone is strong when squeezed but snaps when stretched, so stone beams can only span short gaps. That is why the columns stand so close together — each gap is the longest a stone lintel can safely bridge.

body.heading: Why they swell and lean
paragraphs: Look closely and the columns are not perfectly straight: many bulge very slightly in the middle, a refinement called entasis, and corner columns are a touch thicker and lean inward. These tweaks correct optical illusions that would make a dead-straight temple look pinched and splayed.
The flutes — the vertical grooves — carry the eye upward and emphasise that each column is a load-bearing post, not a wall. The decoration is the structure, made visible.

takeaway: Greek temple columns are a stone skeleton: close-set posts carrying short stone beams, subtly swollen and leaning to look straight while they hold the roof up.
